facts.title: Named for a Continent
facts.text: Europium is one of the few elements named after a continent, taking its name from Europe. It was isolated and identified by the French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay in 1901, who used painstaking fractional crystallization to separate it from samarium. Demarçay suspected an unknown element was hiding in samarium samples studied earlier by Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran and William Crookes.

facts.title: The Softest Lanthanide
facts.text: Europium is the softest and least dense of the rare-earth metals, with a density of about 5.24 grams per cubic centimeter, similar to ordinary glass. It is soft enough to be cut with a knife, and its melting point is a relatively low 826 degrees Celsius. These unusually low values come from its electron structure, where it prefers to keep two electrons for metallic bonding rather than three.

facts.title: The Most Reactive Rare Earth
facts.text: Europium is the most reactive of all the lanthanides, tarnishing almost instantly in air and reacting vigorously with water much like calcium does. For this reason it is usually stored sealed under inert mineral oil or argon to keep it from oxidizing. Freshly cut europium has a bright silvery shine that quickly dulls to a yellowish oxide coat.

facts.title: It Made the Color TV Red
facts.text: Europium revolutionized color television and computer monitors as the source of vivid, pure red light in phosphors. Compounds such as europium-doped yttrium oxide and yttrium oxysulfide glow brilliant red when struck by electrons or ultraviolet light. Before europium phosphors arrived in the 1960s, red was the weakest and dimmest color on screens, holding back overall picture brightness.

facts.title: The Secret in Euro Banknotes
facts.text: Europium compounds are used as an anti-counterfeiting feature in euro banknotes, which is a fitting use given the element's name. Under ultraviolet light, hidden markings on genuine notes fluoresce in characteristic red, green, and blue colors thanks to europium-based pigments. This invisible signature is extremely hard to reproduce, helping authorities quickly distinguish real currency from fakes.

facts.title: Two Faces, Two Colors
facts.text: Europium is unusual because it readily forms two different ions, Eu2+ and Eu3+, and they glow in completely different colors. The Eu3+ ion produces sharp red emission, while Eu2+ typically gives blue or green light depending on its host crystal. This dual personality lets engineers tune europium phosphors across the spectrum, which is why it appears in both red and blue components of fluorescent lamps and LEDs.

facts.title: A Cosmic Fingerprint
facts.text: Astronomers use europium as a tracer to study how heavy elements were forged across the history of the galaxy. Most europium in the universe is thought to be made by the rapid neutron-capture process, or r-process, in extreme events like neutron star mergers. By measuring europium lines in the light of ancient stars, scientists reconstruct when and where these violent element factories operated.

facts.title: Glow-in-the-Dark Safety Signs
facts.text: The eerie, long-lasting glow of modern emergency exit signs and luminous paints comes largely from europium. Strontium aluminate doped with europium absorbs light and then re-emits it slowly for many hours, far outperforming the older zinc sulfide pigments. Because it is non-radioactive, this europium-based phosphor replaced earlier glowing materials that relied on dangerous radioactive substances.

facts.title: A Spy for Doctors and Chemists
facts.text: Europium's sharp, long-lived fluorescence makes it a powerful label in medical and biological testing. In a technique called time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay, europium tags attached to molecules keep glowing after background light has faded, allowing extremely sensitive detection of hormones, viruses, and disease markers. Researchers also use europium compounds as shift reagents in nuclear magnetic resonance to untangle complex molecular structures.

facts.title: No Job in Living Things
facts.text: Despite being scattered through Earth's crust, europium has no known biological role in any plant or animal. It is one of the rarest of the rare earths in nature, with an abundance of only about 2 parts per million in the crust, and it is never found as a free metal. Most commercial europium is extracted from minerals like bastnasite and monazite, where it occurs mixed with other lanthanides that must be carefully separated.
